items.question: Why is ignorance not simply the absence of knowledge?
premises: Ignorance is the term being defined.
If ignorance were mere absence of knowledge, the definition would over-extend.
Absence of knowledge exists even in a clod and similar inert things.
A clod does not undergo transmigration.
items.inference: Therefore ignorance cannot be defined as mere absence of knowledge.
uncertainties: The sandhi in jñānābhāvaścātiprasaṅgataḥ could be segmented in more than one way, but the sense is clear.
items.plain_english: Ignorance is not simply the absence of knowledge, because that would apply too widely. Even a clod lacks knowledge, yet a clod does not wander in transmigration.

items.question: What is ignorance according to the Shiva Sutras?
premises: Ignorance is not mere absence of knowledge.
The knowable reality can be apprehended either fully or partially.
Knowledge that does not manifest the knowable reality in its totality is still a form of knowledge.
items.inference: Therefore ignorance is knowledge that fails to manifest the knowable reality in its fullness, as taught in the Shiva Sutras.
items.plain_english: So ignorance is not a blank absence; it is knowledge that does not reveal the knowable reality in its fullness. This is what the Shiva Sutras teach.

items.question: How do the two Shiva Sutras together explain self, knowledge, and bondage?
premises: One sutra states that consciousness is the self.
Another sutra states that knowledge is bondage.
Read together by connection and separation, the two sutras convey a single meaning.
items.inference: Therefore the paired sutras show that the self is consciousness, while limited knowledge functions as bondage.
uncertainties: The exact sutra numbers are not named in the verse.
items.plain_english: The two sutras, 'Consciousness is the self' and 'Knowledge is bondage,' are meant to be read together. Taken in relation to each other, they show that the self is consciousness, but limited knowledge becomes bondage.

items.question: What does the word 'consciousness' mean in the ancient sutra?
premises: The word 'caitanya' is an abstract noun form.
In the ancient sutra it denotes freedom alone.
It does not bring in any further particular specifications.
items.inference: Therefore in that sutra 'consciousness' means sheer freedom, without added qualifications.
items.plain_english: In the ancient sutra, the word 'consciousness' is used in its abstract sense to mean sheer freedom, without importing any extra particular features.

items.question: How does the second sutra introduce duality into sheer consciousness?
premises: The second sutra speaks of action or instrument.
Sheer consciousness in itself has no such divisions.
Naming action or instrument introduces a distinction.
items.inference: Therefore the second sutra presents duality in what is otherwise sheer consciousness.
items.plain_english: But the second sutra, by speaking of action or instrument, introduces duality into what is in itself sheer consciousness.

items.question: Why is the manifestation of duality called ignorance and bondage?
premises: The manifestation of duality is ignorance.
It is insubstantial.
What is insubstantial bondage must be removed.
items.inference: Therefore dual manifestation is called ignorance and bondage, and for that reason it is to be cut off.
uncertainties: The phrase āvṛttyā nirūpitam may refer to repeated scriptural explanation; the exact reference is not specified.
items.plain_english: The appearance of duality is ignorance. Because it is insubstantial, it is called bondage, and for that very reason it is something to be cut away, as the teaching explains repeatedly.

items.question: If what is other than the free self is empty, can liberation be a separate thing?
premises: Anything other than the free self is empty.
An empty something cannot constitute a real separate liberation.
A real separate liberation would require a distinct name and status.
items.inference: Therefore there is no liberation as a separate entity apart from the free self, not even in name.
items.plain_english: Anything apart from the free self is empty. Since that is so, there is no separate thing called liberation, and it does not even deserve a separate name.

items.question: What kind of knowledge brings about the quieting of transmigration?
premises: The knowable reality can be manifested more and more fully.
Knowledge may correspond to those increasing degrees of fullness.
Greater fullness of manifestation reduces transmigratory bondage.
items.inference: Therefore progressively fuller knowledge of the true knowable reality brings a corresponding quieting of transmigration.
items.plain_english: But knowledge that reveals the true knowable reality more and more fully, step by step, brings a corresponding quieting of transmigration.

items.question: How does limited liberating knowledge free one to a corresponding extent?
premises: One may recognize oneself as untainted, inwardly empty, and devoid of agency.
Such recognition can be held briefly or in detail.
Liberating knowledge works according to its scope.
items.inference: Therefore knowledge of this kind liberates one only to the extent that it is actually realized.
uncertainties: The exact doctrinal nuance of antaḥśūnyaḥ here may vary by tradition; it is rendered as inwardly empty.
items.plain_english: Recognitions such as 'I am untainted by passion, inwardly empty, and without agency,' whether grasped briefly or in detail, do liberate, but only to the extent that such knowledge is actually present.

items.question: When is someone truly liberated rather than only partially liberated?
premises: A person may be freed from one limitation.
That same person may still remain within another limitation.
Complete liberation requires freedom from all limitations.
items.inference: Therefore one who is freed only in part is still not fully liberated, while the truly liberated is free from all limitations.
items.plain_english: So someone may be liberated in one respect and still remain unliberated because another limitation persists. Only one who is free from all limitations is truly liberated.

items.question: What kind of knowledge yields true liberation without remainder?
premises: Some knowledge is still marked by limitations.
Knowledge of the true knowable reality can be free from all limitations.
Where no limitation remains, ignorance has no foothold.
items.inference: Therefore knowledge of the true knowable reality that is free from all limitations leaves no room for ignorance and gives true liberation.
uncertainties: sarvātmanojjhitam is terse; it is taken here as devoid of limitation in every respect.
items.plain_english: But knowledge of the true knowable reality that is free from every limitation leaves no place anywhere for ignorance, and that knowledge gives true liberation.

items.question: How does the Shiva teaching further classify knowledge and ignorance?
premises: Knowledge and ignorance have already been described.
Each of them admits further distinction.
The Shiva teaching distinguishes a personal and a buddhi-based form.
items.inference: Therefore in the Shiva teaching both knowledge and ignorance are each classified as twofold: personal and buddhi-based.
items.plain_english: The nature of knowledge and ignorance described above is further divided in the Shiva teaching: each of them is twofold, as personal and as buddhi-based.

items.question: What is the personal ignorance called mala in the individual?
premises: The person has a form of ignorance specific to itself.
This ignorance is called mala.
It veils the person's own full nature of consciousness and action, which is Shiva-nature.
items.inference: Therefore personal ignorance, called mala, is the veiling of one's own full consciousness-action Shiva-nature.
items.plain_english: In the individual, the ignorance called mala is that which veils one's own full Shiva-nature of consciousness and action. It arises in relation to that very condition and consists in its concealment.

items.question: Why is the bound being's personal ignorance not a function of the intellect?
premises: The bound being's cognition and action are contracted.
This personal ignorance is unconceptualized.
Determination and similar intellectual operations are absent in it.
items.inference: Therefore this ignorance belongs to the bound subject as such and is not a part of the intellect.
items.plain_english: For the bound being, whose seeing and acting are contracted, that ignorance is unconceptualized. It is not a function of the intellect, because determination and similar mental operations are not present there.

items.question: Under what condition does determinate cognition of the form 'I know this thus' arise?
premises: Determinate cognition takes the form 'I know this thus.'
Such cognition depends on reflection arising through the six sheaths.
The six sheaths condition the limited atom.
items.inference: Therefore determinate cognition arises when reflection occurs through the limiting structure of the six sheaths.
uncertainties: The compound ṣaṭkañcukābilāṇūtthapratibimbanato is compressed; the causal chain is interpreted in line with standard Trika doctrine.
items.plain_english: When a determinate cognition arises in the form 'I know this in this way,' it does so through a reflection that comes up from the limited self under the conditioning of the six sheaths.

items.question: How are buddhi-based ignorance and personal ignorance related when determinate intellect arises?
premises: Determinate intellect arises under the conditions described previously.
That determinate cognition is called buddhi-based ignorance.
Personal ignorance stands in a nourishing relation to it.
items.inference: Therefore when determinate intellect arises, buddhi-based ignorance appears, with personal ignorance as what is nourished and buddhi-based ignorance as what nourishes it.
uncertainties: The reciprocal nourishing relation is compactly stated; the verse is read as assigning poṣya/poṣṭṛ roles in that context.
items.plain_english: When that determinate intellect arises, such cognition is called buddhi-based ignorance. In relation to it, the personal ignorance is what is nourished, and the buddhi-based ignorance acts as what nourishes it.

items.question: What kind of knowledge arises when the bound being's latent impressions weaken?
premises: The bound being carries limiting latent impressions.
These impressions can diminish.
A person may reach a higher inner state.
items.inference: Therefore when those latent impressions weaken in a person who has reached the higher state, expansive personal non-conceptual insight arises.
items.plain_english: But when the bound being's latent impressions have weakened and the person has reached a higher state, an expansive personal insight arises, and it is non-conceptual.

items.question: How do personal and buddhi-based knowledge relate when expansive non-conceptual knowledge is present?
premises: Expansive non-conceptual personal knowledge can arise.
Buddhi-based cognition still stands in relation to it.
Their relation follows the fitness of that higher knowledge.
items.inference: Therefore, according to the measure of expansive non-conceptual knowledge, the personal remains what is nourished and the buddhi-based remains what nourishes, as before.
uncertainties: The syntax of yāvasā is compressed; the verse is read as expressing proportional correspondence.
items.plain_english: To the extent that expansive non-conceptual knowledge is fittingly present, the relation remains as before: the personal is what is nourished, and the buddhi-based functions as what nourishes it.

items.question: What is the effect of initiation on personal ignorance and personal knowledge?
premises: Initiation and related rites can destroy personal ignorance.
The destruction of ignorance does not always yield immediate full manifestation.
Personal knowledge may become fully clear at the end of the body.
items.inference: Therefore initiation destroys personal ignorance, yet the corresponding personal knowledge is clearly manifested at the end of that body.
items.plain_english: Through initiation and similar means, personal ignorance is destroyed. Even so, the corresponding personal knowledge becomes clearly manifest at the end of that body.

items.question: When does liberation while living become directly present?
premises: Buddhi-based ignorance can expand and dominate cognition.
Buddhi-based knowledge can dissolve that ignorance.
The removal of that ignorance has an immediate existential effect.
items.inference: Therefore when buddhi-based knowledge dissolves buddhi-based ignorance, liberation while living stands immediately present.
items.plain_english: But when buddhi-based knowledge dissolves the swelling of buddhi-based ignorance, liberation while living is right there, as if placed on the palm of the hand.

items.question: Why is buddhi-based insight primary even in initiation?

Its liberating power depends on being preceded by buddhi-based insight.
What makes initiation effective has primacy in that context.
items.inference: Therefore even in initiation, buddhi-based knowledge has primacy.
items.plain_english: Initiation truly liberates when it is preceded by buddhi-based insight. For that reason, even in initiation, buddhi-based knowledge holds the primary place.

This division appears in authoritative scriptures.
Respected teachers also transmit this division.
items.inference: Therefore the twofold division of knowledge and ignorance is established in the Svayambhuva, Ruru, Matanga, and related texts, and taught by revered teachers such as Khetapala.

items.plain_english: This twofold division within knowledge and ignorance is taught in the Svayambhuva, the Ruru, the Matanga and other texts, and it is upheld by revered teachers such as Khetapala.

items.inference: Therefore scripture is the primary means for attaining such determinate buddhi-based insight.
items.plain_english: For attaining that kind of determinate buddhi-based insight, scripture is primary, because it reveals the knowable reality.

items.question: Why can conceptualization still arise even after initiation removes inner personal ignorance?
premises: Initiation can remove inner personal ignorance.
Conceptual formations may still remain in the intellect.
What remains in the intellect can still give rise to conceptualization.
items.inference: Therefore even after initiation removes inner personal ignorance, conceptualization may still arise because the intellect's residue has not ceased.
items.plain_english: Even if initiation has dissolved inner personal ignorance, conceptualization may still arise, because what remains in the intellect has not yet come to an end.
